title: Planning an investigation
examples: How do I make sure my test is fair?
What are the different kinds of variables I need to check?
What should I write down when I plan an experiment?

explain.say: Today we are learning to plan a physics investigation. A good plan keeps your test fair and safe. We must identify the variables involved first.
The independent variable is what you change on purpose. You decide to change this one thing in your test. For example, you might change the angle of a ramp.
The dependent variable is what you measure to see the result. It depends on what you changed. If you change the angle, you measure the time.
The control variables are everything else that must stay exactly the same. Keeping these constant makes your test fair. For example, the mass of the object must not change.
Next we think about a fair test. A fair test means only one thing changes at a time. This keeps your results reliable and trustworthy. If you change too much, you do not know what caused the result.

faq.q: What is the difference between a variable and a control variable?
faq.a: A variable is anything that can change in your test. A control variable is a specific variable that you must keep exactly the same throughout the whole experiment.
asks: Are control variables the same as controlled variables?

faq.q: Why is it important to write a risk assessment?
faq.a: A risk assessment helps you think about potential dangers before you start. It lets you plan safety steps to prevent accidents during your practical work.
asks: Do I need to check for dangers?
What is the purpose of assessing risk?

faq.q: If I change two things, is my test still fair?
faq.a: No, if you change two things, your test is not fair. You will not know which change caused the result you see. You must only change one thing at a time.
asks: Can I test two things at once?

faq.q: What should I do if I cannot keep a variable constant?
faq.a: If you cannot keep a variable constant, you should mention this limitation in your write-up. It shows that you understand the limits of your test design.
asks: What if my control variable changes?
How do I report a problem with my setup?

faq.q: How do I structure my method section?
faq.a: Your method should be written as a clear set of steps. Use numbered points so someone else can repeat your experiment exactly as you did it.
asks: What is the best way to write my steps?
Should I use bullet points for my method?

facts: The independent variable is the factor that is deliberately changed by the experimenter.
The dependent variable is the factor that is measured or observed during the experiment.
A fair test requires that all variables, except the independent one, are kept constant.
A risk assessment identifies potential hazards and suggests ways to reduce those risks.

quiz.say: In an experiment testing how temperature affects the speed of a reaction, what is the temperature?
quiz.why: You are changing the temperature on purpose to see what happens.

wrong.1: This is wrong because you are measuring the speed, not the temperature.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you are actively changing the temperature in this test.
wrong.3: This is too general; the variable name is more specific.

quiz.say: To test how the length of a pendulum string affects its period, what must you keep the same?
quiz.why: The mass must stay the same to ensure only the length is affecting the period.

wrong.0: While this is a control variable, the mass is a more critical constant here.
wrong.2: This is the variable you are intentionally changing.
wrong.3: This is what you are measuring, the dependent variable.

quiz.say: Which statement shows a fair test design?
quiz.show: One thing changes at a time

options.show: Changing only the voltage while keeping the length constant.
options.say: Changing only the voltage while keeping the length constant.

quiz.why: This correctly identifies one variable changing while others are controlled.

wrong.0: Changing two things makes the test unfair because of two different factors.
wrong.1: This describes only measuring, not designing a test that changes something.
wrong.3: Changing two things at once means you cannot tell what caused the result.
